label: sequence started with q: late original-phase steps (t>=4) through <DEL>
explanation: Fires on sequences whose first original token is q (96% of activation mass), at every original-phase step from t=4 (weakly at t=3) through the <DEL> step, whatever the current input token is. It is essentially silent during the copy phase (10 activations), including while q is being output. Magnitude builds over the original phase, is largest around orig_idx 4-7, and drops somewhat at <DEL>. Sequences that also have q as the second token are overrepresented among the strongest activations. Remaining misses are weak (about 4% of mass): sequences with q at position 1 instead of position 0 give faint activations, and t=3 gives moderate ones. With t>=4 the predicate has about 0.997 precision on dev. It does not fire on sequences without an early q.

issues: The core claims check out on the test split. Precision is 0.997, and silence in the copy phase holds (10 dev activations, all at recall_idx 1-3). The original-phase part alone (phase 0, q first, t>=4) has precision 0.998, and <DEL> with q first has precision 0.973. A second q in the sequence does not suppress firing (precision 0.98).

There is a systematic class of misses that the explanation describes wrongly. Count recall is only 0.739, and the predicate covers only 10% of the bottom activation quartile. Most of the missed active steps come from sequences where q is the SECOND original token (orig(1)=='q', t>=5). That class alone covers about 15% of all active test steps.

That q-at-position-1 class depends on what the first token is. It is not just 'faint activations'. With orig(1)=='q' and t>=5, precision is about 0.55-0.71 when the first token is a, c, e, f, l, u, w, y, 0 or 1. It is exactly 0 when the first token is h, i, j, k or r, and close to 0 for m, o, p, s, t, z or 2. So it is a gated secondary trigger, not uniform weak leakage.

The explanation says the remaining misses hold 'about 4% of mass'. The misses tool on the test split reports 6.8% of activation mass in missed steps (20,208 steps), and the bottom quartile of activations is almost entirely uncovered.
There is also a t=3 class of misses, as the explanation admits. Extending the predicate to t>=3 lowers precision to 0.86, so that onset is only partial.
Caveat on the better predicate: I picked its first-token set by looking at test-split counts, so its F1 of 0.879 (vs 0.849) is somewhat optimistic.
skeptic.revised_label: q early in the sequence: late original-phase steps through <DEL>. Mainly sequences that start with q (t>=4). Weaker secondary firing when q is the second token and the first token is from a specific set (e.g. a/c/e/f/l/u/w/y/0/1). Silent in the copy phase.

final_label: q early in the sequence: late original-phase steps through <DEL>. Mainly sequences that start with q (t>=4). Weaker secondary firing when q is the second token and the first token is from a specific set (e.g. a/c/e/f/l/u/w/y/0/1). Silent in the copy phase.

scorecard.summary: Graded preference over the first original token (most: q, l, w, 1, e, a; least: m, h, j, i) and the third original token (most: j, r, m, i, t, 0; least: w, l, q, 3); timing cues that raise it most: t=5, t=6, t=4.
